response = "The problem began with a measurement rather than a theory. Urbain Le Verrier reported in 1859 that Mercury's perihelion advanced faster than Newtonian theory predicted; that is, Mercury's perihelion advances by about 43 arcseconds per century beyond the Newtonian prediction. The residual was tiny, but it was stubborn under every refinement of the planetary tables, and it set the terms of a debate that occupied celestial mechanics for half a century. Because Le Verrier had earlier used orbital anomalies of Uranus to predict the existence of Neptune, he was brought to propose that an unseen intra-Mercurial planet or ring of matter caused the excess precession of Mercury's perihelion. In other words, the excess precession arises from unmodelled mass lying inside Mercury's orbit. At least one of two accounts of the residual must hold, and perhaps both: unmodelled mass inside Mercury's orbit, or a defect in the law of gravitation itself. Edmond Lescarbault's report of a transiting dark object was made in 1878. Repeated eclipse searches, by contrast, failed to yield any confirmable sighting of an intra-Mercurial planet, and that long series of negative results indicates that no intra-Mercurial planet has ever been confirmed to exist. Either the record stands at that want of confirmation, or a planet orbiting inside Mercury's orbit was confirmed by later telescopic observation; one of the two is the case, and they cannot both be. Dynamical reasoning then narrowed the matter decisively, for a body massive enough to produce the observed precession would also have perturbed the node and inclination of Mercury's orbit detectably, which indicates that the excess precession arises from a deficiency in Newton's law of gravitation. Before the theoretical question could be pressed, the reality of the residual itself had to be secured. Simon Newcomb's analysis of the planetary tables concluded that the perihelion residual was genuine and not a product of computational error in the planetary perturbations. The entire anomaly was an artifact of arithmetic errors in Le Verrier's tables of Venus. A residual that survives independent recomputation and a figure manufactured wholly by arithmetic slips in the Venus tables cannot both be true of the same 43 arcseconds per century. The resolution came from gravitational theory. Albert Einstein derived a perihelion advance of 43 arcseconds per century from general relativity in November 1915, a value that follows from the field equations for a test particle near a spherical mass without any adjustable constant fitted to Mercury. Because the number emerged from the structure of the theory rather than from a free parameter, the agreement with the measured advance was treated as a decisive test, and the search for intra-Mercurial matter ceased to be the natural way of accounting for the motion of Mercury's perihelion."
